data.title: County officials sue Fincen over beneficial ownership rule
data.description:
• Key insight: Two Democratic county prosecutors filed a lawsuit arguing the Trump administration’s move to effectively shutter a reporting regime meant to combat shell companies harms law enforcement and has not been adequately justified by the agency. 
  • Expert quote: “The statute plainly does not contemplate an exemption for all domestic companies from reporting requirements. By FinCEN’s own estimation, Defendants have exempted over 99% of the entities previously mandated to report beneficial ownership information under the [Corporate Transparency Act].” — Laura Conover of Pima County, Arizona, and Mary Moriarty of Hennepin County, Minnesota

data.title: Fed’s Cook questions whether one rate cut is enough
data.description:

data.title: Press Release Brazil’s Daycoval Selects Temenos SaaS to Power its US Expansion
data.description:
Temenos (SIX: TEMN), a global leader in banking technology, today announced that Banco Daycoval S.A. (Daycoval), a major Brazilian bank specializing in corporate lending, has selected Temenos SaaS on Microsoft Azure to drive its international expansion in the United States.

Daycoval will initially adopt services including core banking, digital onboarding and financial crime mitigation on Temenos SaaS, later adding payments and trade finance capabilities, as the bank seeks to better support its corporate clients operating internationally.

Ranked among Brazil’s top 20 banks by total assets, Daycoval is a well-established and diversified financial institution with a nationwide presence and a comprehensive range of financial products and services. The bank combines its core business of lending to companies with selected retail banking activities, while steadily expanding its presence in capital markets and investment banking. 

Founded in 1968, Daycoval has approximately 4,500 employees and in the first nine months of 2026 reported recurring net income of R$1.36 billion and ROAE of 23.8%.  Its expanded loan portfolio reached R$80.1 billion at the end of September, up 24.4% YoY, while total funding stood at R$80.2 billion. Asset quality remained sound, with a 90-day NPL ratio at 2.2%. Additionally, the Bank’s Basel Capital Ratio increased 150bps QoQ to 14.3%.

Daycoval already has an international presence through its branch in the Cayman Islands and recently received conditional approval to open a federal branch in the United States. Through the new branch, Daycoval initially plans to offer corporate deposit accounts, bilateral and external lending, and domestic and international payments, further strengthening its offering for corporate clients engaged in international business, particularly those seeking to expand in the United States.

With Temenos SaaS, Daycoval will benefit from a comprehensive set of banking services, including capabilities tailored to the needs of the US market, delivered on a single platform that will help the bank reduce integration risk. Temenos’ flexible, cloud-native solution will enable Daycoval to scale efficiently and add new capabilities progressively as its US operations expand.

Adopting a SaaS model, with updates, support and maintenance handled by Temenos, will empower Daycoval to focus on its customers, rather than on managing its technology. Meanwhile, Temenos’ open, API-based architecture will enable seamless integration with other bank systems and third-party solutions, helping it to launch new products rapidly and deliver an enhanced digital experience. 

Paulo Saba, Investor Relations Senior Officer, Banco Daycoval S.A., said: “Establishing a branch in the United States is a key pillar of our international expansion strategy, enabling Daycoval to better support the international operations of our longstanding clients”. 

Marta Alves, General Manager, Banco Daycoval S.A. (Miami Branch), added “Temenos’ proven capabilities and flexible, cloud-native platform will enable us to establish our US presence quickly and scale efficiently as our business evolves, supporting disciplined and sustainable growth.”

Rodrigo Silva, President, Latin America, Temenos said: “We’re delighted that Daycoval has chosen Temenos SaaS for its expansion into the US. This is a clear vote of confidence in Temenos’ capabilities for the US market, as well as further evidence of our growing momentum in Brazil. We look forward to helping Daycoval to meet the evolving needs of its international corporate clients with agility and speed on Temenos SaaS.”

About Temenos

Temenos (SIX: TEMN) is a global leader in banking technology. Through our market-leading core banking suite and best-in-class composable solutions, we are modernizing the banking industry. Banks of all sizes utilize our adaptable technology – on-premises, in the cloud, or as SaaS – to deliver next-generation services and AI-enhanced experiences that elevate banking for their customers. Our mission is to create a world where people can live their best financial lives.

For more information, please visit www.temenos.com.

data.title: BankThink Washington could learn a lot from Europe on crypto regulation
data.description:
• Key insight: Unlike in the U.S., where the crypto industry has endured regulation-by-enforcement for most of a decade, Europe has made real strides toward a rules-based order. Policymakers in Washington should take note.
  • Forward look: Washington should not read Europe’s experience simply as a cautionary tale about overregulation. The U.S. could be seen as a cautionary tale for under-regulating, which has led to regulation by enforcement for over a decade, encouraging legitimate businesses to stay offshore.

Europe gets a bad rap in tech. The “regulate rather than innovate” criticism has become so overused that it’s nearly meaningless. And while it’s true that Europe has slower growth than America, there are certain areas where regulation makes sense.

data.title: Q&A: Maxine Waters talks priorities for House committee
data.description:
WASHINGTON — When Democrats swept the 2026 midterm elections, the party regained a solid control of Congress and the gavels of committees that oversee and make rules for banks. 

In the House, that means Rep. Maxine Waters is back. The tenured lawmaker has represented her California district for three and a half decades, and has been the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee for 13 years. While she’s a familiar, if not always a friendly, face behind the podium for the nation’s banks, she’s joined by progressive allies like Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who’s next in line to lead the Senate Banking Committee, and enjoys support from her caucus to dig into the Trump administration and its financial relationships with private companies.

data.title: Fired NCUA board members continue long-shot legal fight
data.description:
• What’s at stake: If the two fired NCUA officials lose their case, the ruling will further crystallize the new reality that presidents can terminate most agency heads without cause.
  • Expert quote: “In the long term, the NCUA, just like any other agency at this point, would be more subject to political headwinds and changes in the administration.” — Ann Petros, managing counsel for America’s Credit Unions

Two credit-union regulators fired by President Trump appear likely to lose their fight in court, cementing a more partisan future for the National Credit Union Administration. Some industry advocates say that would be a defeat not just for the two officials, but for credit unions in general.

data.title: Barr says Fed downsizing could hamper response to future crises
data.description:
• Key insight: The former Fed vice chair for supervision said recent changes to supervision and regulation are not contributing to near-term risks, but could make it harder to respond to issues in the future.
  • Expert quote: “One of the problems that happened in the global financial crisis is the Fed didn’t have enough talent focused on these issues in Washington to understand at a deep enough level fast enough what was going on. The Federal Reserve’s former chief regulator is worried the central bank could be repeating one of its key failings from the 2008 financial crisis: having too few experts on hand to address it.

data.title: JPMorgan, Visa warn of cyberattack that hit outside vendor
data.description:
(Bloomberg) — JPMorgan Chase & Co., Visa Inc. and Mastercard Inc. said some customer information was accessed in a cyberattack on a vendor.

JPMorgan said it believes, based on an investigation so far, that hackers accessed marketing data held by an outside firm, which may include customer names and email addresses. The bank said the issue isn’t related to an outage it faced earlier this week.

data.title: The link between ‘patchmegeddon’ and recent tech outages
data.description:
Key insight: Many experts have landed on a theory that several ill-explained outages over the past week were caused by hasty software patching in reaction to the release of frontier models that expose xero-day vulnerabilities faster than most companies can fix them.

Expert quote: “I think Patchmegeddon is a plausible explanation for at least some of these outages, although I’d be hesitant to connect it directly to Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase, or others without more evidence. Who knows what’s really going on anymore?” —Bradley Leimer, strategic advisor at Darrery Capital and former head of innovation at Santander, told American Banker.

data.title: Jefferson: inflation must return to 2% before Fed changes target
data.description:
• Key insight: The Fed’s second in command is not willing to entertain a change in inflation target at this time.
  • Expert quote: “I am fully committed to the 2% target as our policy objective. I think that’s critical for finding a nominal anchor, and it’s key to our accountability and our credibility. I would not be interested in entertaining discussion of some other target or target range unless we achieve that 2% target for a durable and extended period of time.” — Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson

The Federal Reserve is considering a host of changes to its monetary policy framework, but for the central bank’s second in command, at least one component remains off the table: the 2% inflation target.
